cls: Progestogen-only oral contraceptive (progestin; desogestrel 75 microgram mini-pill)
pharm: Progestogen (prodrug of etonogestrel) that primarily inhibits ovulation and thickens cervical mucus, providing contraception without estrogen.
quick: One 75 microgram tablet daily, continuously, at the same time each day
May be taken with or without food
Not indicated in pregnancy; stop if pregnancy confirmed
Blood pressure, bleeding pattern, pregnancy if amenorrhoeic
summary: Desogestrel 75 micrograms is an estrogen-free progestogen-only oral contraceptive (the desogestrel mini-pill, e.g., Cerazette/Cerelle). Unlike traditional progestogen-only pills that rely mainly on cervical-mucus effects, the desogestrel dose is high enough to inhibit ovulation in most cycles, giving efficacy comparable to combined pills. It is taken continuously, one tablet every day at about the same time with no pill-free interval; a tablet is considered missed if more than 12 hours late. It is suitable when estrogen is contraindicated, including during breastfeeding. Irregular bleeding is the most common side effect. Enzyme-inducing drugs reduce its effectiveness. It is approved in the EU/UK and many countries but is not FDA-approved in the United States as a single-ingredient product (data are from the EMA/SmPC and BNF).
indications: Contraception (prevention of pregnancy) in women, including those for whom estrogen-containing contraceptives are unsuitable and during breastfeeding

dosage.d: One 75 microgram tablet once daily, taken continuously without a break, at about the same time each day
dosage.n: Start on day 1 of the cycle (or per switching instructions); no tablet-free interval

dosage.d: Take the missed tablet as soon as remembered and the next at the usual time; contraceptive protection maintained
dosage.n: Less than 12 hours late = still protected

dosage.d: Take the most recent missed tablet, continue daily, and use an additional barrier method for the next 7 days
dosage.n: More than 12 hours late reduces protection

admin: Take one tablet at about the same time every day so the interval between tablets is always 24 hours
Take continuously - there is no pill-free week
If a tablet is more than 12 hours late, use additional barrier contraception for 7 days
If vomiting occurs within 3-4 hours of taking a tablet or with severe diarrhoea, follow missed-tablet advice
May be taken with or without food
moa: Desogestrel is a progestogen that is rapidly converted to its active metabolite etonogestrel. At the 75 microgram dose, its principal contraceptive mechanism is inhibition of ovulation, suppressing the mid-cycle luteinising hormone surge. It also thickens cervical mucus, impeding sperm penetration, and alters the endometrium. Because it contains no estrogen, it avoids estrogen-related risks and is suitable for women in whom estrogen is contraindicated or who are breastfeeding.

absolute: Severe or active hepatic disease (until liver function returns to normal)
Known or suspected sex-steroid-sensitive malignancies (e.g., certain breast cancers)
Hypersensitivity to desogestrel or any component
relative: History of ectopic pregnancy or tubal disease
History of breast cancer (with caution per specialist advice)
monitor: Bleeding pattern and possibility of pregnancy if amenorrhoea occurs
Persistent or new lower abdominal pain (consider ectopic pregnancy)

preg: Desogestrel is not indicated during pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs or is suspected during use, the tablets should be stopped; available data on inadvertent exposure have not indicated an increased risk of birth defects.
lact: Desogestrel may be used during breastfeeding. Small amounts of etonogestrel are excreted in breast milk (an estimated 0.01-0.05 micrograms/kg/day ingested by the infant); studies have not shown adverse effects on the growth or development of breastfed infants.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is recommended for renal impairment.
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe or active hepatic disease; do not use until liver function values have returned to normal. Steroid hormones may be poorly metabolised in hepatic impairment.

major: Hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs (rifampicin, rifabutin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, and certain antiretrovirals) - increase clearance and reduce contraceptive efficacy
St John's Wort (Hypericum) - reduces contraceptive efficacy
moderate: Some HIV/HCV protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors - may increase or decrease progestin levels
Certain antiepileptics (e.g., topiramate, oxcarbazepine) - may reduce efficacy
minor: Activated charcoal may reduce absorption if taken close together
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect some laboratory tests (e.g., binding proteins, hepatic/thyroid markers); usually within normal range.

emergency: Signs of venous thromboembolism (calf pain/swelling, sudden breathlessness, chest pain)
Severe lower abdominal pain (possible ectopic pregnancy)

monitoring: Bleeding pattern; exclude pregnancy if unexpected amenorrhoea
New or persistent lower abdominal pain (ectopic pregnancy)
Mood, particularly in women with a history of depression
Glucose control in women with diabetes
counsel: Take one tablet at the same time every day with no break between packs
If you are more than 12 hours late with a tablet, take it and use condoms for the next 7 days
Irregular bleeding or no periods is common and usually not harmful - tell your doctor if it is heavy or worrying
Tell your doctor if you take medicines for epilepsy, tuberculosis, or take St John's Wort, as they can stop the pill working
If you vomit within a few hours of a tablet or have severe diarrhoea, treat it like a missed pill
Seek urgent care for severe one-sided lower belly pain or signs of a blood clot
pk: Ovulation inhibition develops over the first cycle; protection from day 1 start
Etonogestrel plasma Tmax ~1.8 hours after a dose
Once-daily dosing; steady state in 4-5 days
Do not store above 30 C; keep in original packaging
pearls: Higher progestin dose than classic mini-pills allows ovulation inhibition, giving combined-pill-like efficacy
Estrogen-free - useful when estrogen is contraindicated and during breastfeeding
12-hour missed-pill window (vs 3 hours for traditional progestogen-only pills)
Irregular bleeding is the most common reason for discontinuation - counsel up front
Enzyme inducers and St John's Wort reduce efficacy - advise additional barrier protection
Not FDA-approved as a single-ingredient product in the US (data from EMA/SmPC and BNF); marketed as Cerazette/Cerelle in the EU/UK
missed: A tablet is missed if it is more than 12 hours late. If less than 12 hours late, take it at once and continue normally - protection is maintained. If more than 12 hours late, take the most recently missed tablet, continue daily, and use a barrier method (e.g., condoms) for the next 7 days.
overdose: There have been no reports of serious harmful effects from overdose. Symptoms that may occur include nausea, vomiting, and, in young girls, slight vaginal bleeding. There is no antidote; treatment is symptomatic and supportive.
